prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews lyric, essay and narrative through hybrid forms and an exacting, long-running dialogue with antiquity, joining erudition to exposed feeling

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Anne Carson (B002) alone. The round-1 exchange sharpened the grounds but did not alter them. The case rests on the writing. Her voice is recognisable in a few lines, with its dry syntax, abrupt turns and exposed feeling under scholarly exactness. In Autobiography of Red the Geryon material, reached through the fragments of Stesichorus, becomes a verse novel with its own erotic and emotional logic. In Nox the elegy for a brother is made from translation, philological commentary and archival fragments, so the form carries the grief. The hybrid practice is a single exacting poetics and not a convenience. It continues through the lyric essays, the verse and the stagings of Greek drama. It also relates to a tradition I know from my own scholarly field, that of the fragment and of writing with and against loss, but I treat that as context and not as evidence. On maturity, I take the chair's round-1 question seriously. From public knowledge only, and without having verified the texts, I would point to books after Nox, such as the return to the Geryon material in Red Doc> and the later verse and performance-oriented volumes, as the places where continuing invention or repetition must be tested. I cannot settle that from the supplied evidence. I therefore do not claim a late phase I cannot verify, and I would let the citation rest on the demonstrated core: the verse novel, the lyric essay, the elegiac book and the sustained dialogue with antiquity. I do not count the six-of-six agreement in round 1 as a literary argument. It shows only that the writer is the same, not that the grounds are tested. For me the case holds because the formal solution is original, the project coheres across decades, and the emotional and intellectual depth survives the loss of the page-design effects better than one might fear.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still maturity and scale. Much of Carson's work is short, fragmentary or object-like, so the claim of sustained significance rests on cumulative renewal of a method and not on one large architecture, as it would for Cărtărescu's Solenoid or Zurita's sequences. If a close reading showed that her later books refine a settled manner without deepening it, the maturity case would weaken, and I would move toward Cărtărescu (B042) on literary grounds of scale, coherence and the extension of his materials. A second objection is that part of the effect depends on typography, page design and Greek allusion, which are hard to judge in translation. A third is that the line between scholarship, translation and original writing is not settled, especially in Nox, where translation is part of the elegiac method. A last caution is that my own assessment, like every colleague's, rests on public knowledge of a corpus whose most recent decade I know poorly. Readability in English is a fact about evidence and not a merit argument, and I would not let it stand in for the comparison.

responses.point: Mattson holds that sustained development is better tested by the sequence from Autobiography of Red to Nox and beyond than by any one book, and that if continuing invention cannot be established it should count against Carson and be said openly. She also proposes Cărtărescu as the move if a close reading shows only refinement of a method.
responses.response: I accept that rule and apply it to myself. If the later books cannot be shown to extend the project, the committee should say so in the maturity assessment, and I would not paper over it with the first-ranked count. Where I differ is on what counts as evidence of development. I read the return to earlier material in new formal shapes, and the movement from verse novel to elegiac object to drama, as potentially developmental. But that is a claim about specific volumes that I have not verified. So I hold the same conditional you do: the case stands on the demonstrated core, and a shown repetition would shift my balance toward B042. I would ask that the final citation avoid any claim about a late phase that colleagues cannot support.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that in Nox translation is itself the elegiac method, so the line between original writing and translation cannot simply be drawn. He therefore frames the citation around the encounter between antiquity and modern experience and not around genre.
responses.response: This is the most useful correction to my round-1 wording. I said the translations and scholarship should be context and not the basis of the citation, and I still hold that for the translated Greek volumes and the academic prose as such. In Nox, however, the act of translating Catullus is part of the elegy, so it belongs to the original work. I would therefore fix the citation scope as follows: Carson's own books, including those that incorporate translation as a compositional method, are credited, while stand-alone translations and scholarship are not the grounds. That wording keeps the prize from being read as one for erudition and also does not cut Nox in half. I think your encounter between antiquity and modern experience is the right frame, and it is why I keep 'dialogue with antiquity' in the citation.

responses.point: Sward wants the citation to name the seriousness about grief, desire and inheritance explicitly, so that it does not read as a prize for erudition alone. She also argues that sustained quality is not the same as volume.
responses.response: I agree on the first point and have adjusted the wording to meet it by ending the citation on 'joining erudition to exposed feeling', which puts the feeling in the credited grounds and not only the learning. On volume I agree that length does not make a body of work sustained. But I would not let that settle the comparison with Cărtărescu and Zurita, because their case is not about length alone. It is about whether a large, coherent structure shows depth of a different kind than repeated formal renewal. I regard that as open, not as a point against you. My answer is that Carson's recurrent concerns, visible across decades and across forms, make a coherent oeuvre. But the committee should test that against individual volumes, as you said, before the citation is fixed.

responses.point: Palm names Autobiography of Red and Nox as the core where the formal reinvention is fullest, and sees Cărtărescu's late phase, Solenoid in particular, as evidence of continued ambition. She keeps him second, noting the risk of repetition in the very long novels and the exposure of his sentence-level texture to translation.
responses.response: I take your account of the core as the working scope of the citation. On Cărtărescu, I agree that Solenoid is a strong maturity argument and that the risk of repetition and of translation loss is real in a prose whose force lies at sentence level. That is why I do not move him first: I cannot judge the Romanian, and an unverifiable loss in translation is a reason for caution, not a reason to dismiss him. It is also why I would not let access to English settle the matter. If the committee had a reliable reading of his Romanian that showed the translations understate him, I would reopen the order, and I want that stated as the condition and not as a hint of a change. As of now I keep B042 as my first alternative, ahead of B005, on the scale and coherence of the project.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any text. My knowledge of Carson's work after Nox, including Red Doc> and the later verse and performance pieces, is general public knowledge, and I cannot say whether these books deepen the project or repeat it.
How far her typographic, book-object and performance pieces can be judged as literature, and how her allusive and page-dependent forms travel into Swedish and other languages, remains unresolved.

Where the line falls between original writing, translation and scholarship, especially in Nox, is a judgment the committee must make explicitly. My proposed scope credits her own books that use translation as method and leaves stand-alone translations and scholarship as context.
Whether cumulative scale (Cărtărescu, Zurita) or repeated formal renewal (Carson) better demonstrates sustained achievement is not settled by the supplied evidence.
For Cărtărescu and Zurita, translation losses at the level of the sentence and line, thin translated coverage of the poetry, and the status of Zurita's landscape works as literature are uncertain.

The shortlist gives only two representative works per writer, so any whole-oeuvre claim rests on general public knowledge. Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption, since her actual committee voting status is undocumented.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly work on the literary fragment, exile literature and Celan overlaps thematically with some candidates' concerns, and I treat that as context only, not as a tie to any candidate. The profile lists no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to Carson or any other shortlisted writer. As chair I wrote the round-1 summary, which is a process record and not a ruling, and I have kept my own position separate from it here. Ceremony speeches I have given express the Academy's collective position and are not evidence of my vote.
